Full text

Abstract

People report as memories not only what they retrieve, but what seems plausible. Routine knowledge may inform plausibility judgments and support accurate reconstruction when behavior follows an expected routine. But how often does behavior match those routine expectations? We conducted preregistered analyses of previously collected longitudinal data from student and community samples (N = 207;Cárdenas et al., 2021). We compared expected routines for 18,736 day-and-hour periods-e.g., Tuesdays, 1-2 PM-with 3,510 one-time experience-sampled occasions and 725 retrospective reports. Participants expected complete routines during 92.83% of waking-hour periods, but behavior matched at least two of three expected domains on only 44.39% of occasions expected to be highly typical. Expected typicality did not reliably predict recall accuracy. Exploratorily, higher expected typicality predicted greater schema reliance: retrospective reports reproduced expectations that had not matched sampled behavior. Routine knowledge may provide a less reliable basis for reconstruction than participants' confidence in their routines suggests.

The Illusion of Routine Knowledge: Time-Specific Expectations Weakly Predict Behavior on Sampled Occasions

People are sometimes asked to account for an ordinary moment in their pasts. A romantic partner may ask where the other was one evening, while a doctor may ask what a patient was doing when symptoms began. A detective may ask a suspect or corroborator for an alibi at a particular time. Errors in autobiographical recall can contribute to interpersonal strain (Ray et al., 2019), clinical errors (Redelmeier et al., 2001), and wrongful convictions when inaccurate alibis appear deceptive (Crozier et al., 2017). Yet mundane everyday moments may not be encoded with later retrieval in mind (Brewer, 1988), leaving people to reconstruct what likely happened from expectations about what usually happens at that time (Barclay, 1986; Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000). To evaluate this strategy, we use naturalistic experience sampling to examine whether time-specific routine expectations-expectations about what usually happens during recurring day-and-hour time periods (e.g., Tuesdays, 1-2 PM)-match sampled behavior and inform later reconstruction.

People may base reconstruction on schemas, which represent common features of repeated experiences (Bartlett, 1932; Ghosh & Gilboa, 2014). In everyday life, people may draw on generalized knowledge of repeated personal experiences and familiar event scripts to form expectations about where they are usually found, what they usually do, with whom, and, critically, at what specific times (Brewer, 1986; Schank & Abelson, 1977). By providing a framework for what is expected, schemas guide how people perceive, remember, and interpret information (Rubínová & Kontogianni, 2023). Indeed, research suggests that people perceive much of everyday behavior as habitual and view routines as a pervasive feature of daily life (Rebar et al., 2026). For example, recent work found that adults estimated that most of their own and others' waking hours followed routines that "repeated with some degree of regularity usually at approximately the same days and times with few exceptions" (Mdn = 70%, SD = 18.41; Thy et al., 2025). However, prior work has not examined how often people expect routines during particular day-and-hour periods or mapped those expectations to reality. If people hold a strong perception of regularity for most waking hours, and such perceptions are accurate, knowledge about one's routines may provide an efficient basis for inferring what likely happened when episodic memory is weak or unavailable. Conversely, schema-based inference is also risky because it can lead people to substitute expectation for actual experience (Brewer & Treyens, 1981; Lampinen et al., 2001; Nakamura et al., 1985; Neuschatz et al., 2002). When what usually happens fails to happen at the expected time, or fails to happen altogether, reconstructions may produce reports that are consistent with the schema for that time period rather than with what actually occurred (Leins & Charman, 2016). This risk may be especially likely for repeated behaviors, because memory often preserves the general pattern of recurring events better than the details that distinguish one occurrence from another (Dilevski et al., 2022; Rubínová & Kontogianni, 2023). Timespecific cues do not always solve this problem, because ordinary events are often weakly encoded with respect to when they occurred (Friedman, 1993; Thompson et al., 1993).

When direct recollection is weak, memory reports depend not only on what people retrieve, but also on how they evaluate candidate events before deciding whether to report them (Koriat & Goldsmith, 1996). Metacognitive models of autobiographical belief suggest that this evaluative process draws on inferential cues-including perceived event prevalence, plausibility, and script knowledge (Mazzoni & Hanczakowski, 2011; Mazzoni & Kirsch, 2002; Scoboria et al., 2014; Scoboria et al., 2006; Scoboria et al., 2004). If beliefs about the frequency and stability of one's routines are strong, they may make routine-consistent events seem especially plausible.

Yet if those beliefs are poorly calibrated to reality, routine-based reconstruction may systematically replace actual behavior with expected behavior. This issue has significant implications for the high-stakes context of criminal investigations (Charman & Shambaugh, 2022). Innocent suspects are often asked to account for a specific past moment that, given their lack of involvement with the crime, was likely ordinary and therefore unlikely to have been encoded in a way that would support its retrieval (Crozier et al., 2017). Laboratory-based experiments show that innocent suspects often rely on schematic knowledge of their routines to generate alibis (Eastwood et al., 2021). This reliance is sometimes helpful: Alibis for schema-consistent occasions tend to be more accurate than alibis for schema-inconsistent occasions (Leins & Charman, 2016).

However, schemas may not always cue actual episodic memories. In Cárdenas et al. (2021), alibis for schema-consistent occasions did not reliably show stronger subjective markers of recollective experience, such as vividness, confidence, or remember/know judgments. Nor were these markers reliably associated with recall accuracy. Accuracy likewise did not vary with the delay between event occurrence and recall, despite substantial evidence linking longer delays with poorer recall accuracy (Murre & Dros, 2015). These results suggest that some schema-consistent alibis may reflect routine knowledge rather than direct memory for the target event. Critically, reliance on routine knowledge can also backfire, leading people to report expected behaviors when they instead engaged in unexpected behaviors (Cárdenas et al., 2021; Eastwood et al., 2021; Leins & Charman, 2016). This work shows that people rely on routine knowledge when reconstructing the past, but it says much less about whether people's expectations about their routines are often accurate enough to justify that use, or about how often routine-consistent versus routine-inconsistent situations occur in the first place.

Research Overview

Using previously unreported longitudinal data collected by Cárdenas and colleagues (2021), we link prospective, concurrent, and retrospective reports to investigate three questions.

First, how often do people expect routines for particular day-and-hour periods? Second, when people expect a day-and-hour period to be highly routine, how often does their behavior on a subsequently sampled occasion align with that expectation? Third, does higher expected typicality predict the accuracy of later reports about those sampled occasions? An expected routine comprises the person, action, and setting details anticipated to recur during that period.

A sampled occasion is one real-time instance of that period. We predicted that time-specific routine expectations would be common but often fail to match sampled occasions. We further predicted that expected typicality would weakly predict how closely sampled behavior matched expected routines, but not recall accuracy.

Method

Design and Participants

We report novel analyses of a newly wrangled dataset drawn from two closely related longitudinal studies conducted by Cárdenas and colleagues (2021). Study 1 collected data from November 15, 2017 (Time 1) through February 26, 2018 (Time 3). Study 2 collected data from March 28, 2018 (Time 1) through May 29, 2018 (Time 4); the researchers avoided holidays during Time 2 sampling. Both studies followed similar procedures and used the same measures through Time 3, as such we pooled all available observations across studies. Participants were recruited for a study ostensibly on sleep and emotional well-being. At Time 1, they reported expected routines for recurring time periods via Qualtrics survey. At Time 2, they reported their concurrent behavior during an approximately 10-day experience sampling phase via textmessaging. At Time 3, they retrospectively reported their behavior during four Time 2 sampled occasions. Study 1 participants completed Time 3 remotely through Qualtrics, whereas Study 2 participants completed Time 3 during a laboratory interview. Study 2 added a second retrospective report at Time 4. Both studies relied on convenience samples of undergraduate students from an urban commuter college in the northeastern United States; however, to further increase demographic diversity, Study 2 broadened recruitment to include local community members. Compensation of up to $50 was prorated based on completion of each study phase.

Across source studies, at Time 1, 207 participants (Study 1: n = 99, Study 2: n = 108) provided 18,736 prospective reports of expected routines for time periods. This exceeded the 152-sample size we anticipated in our preregistration because the available data included participants who provided at least one Time 1 response, not only those classified by Cárdenas et al. (2021) as completing Time 1 (Supplemental Material S1). Retaining these participants was nevertheless consistent with our preregistered plan to use all data available at each phase (Supplemental Material S1).

At Time 2, 144 participants (Study 1: n = 76, Study 2: n = 68) reported their behavior on 3,510 concurrently sampled occasions. At Time 3, 134 (Study 1: n = 74, Study 2: n = 60) provided 507 retrospective reports about selected sampled occasions. In Study 2 only, at Time 4, 58 participants provided a second set of 218 retrospective reports about the same occasions from Time 3. See Figure 1. Differences in sample size reflect attrition across study phases. For retention, demographic, and sample-type analyses, see Supplemental Materials S2-S4.

The current study adds previously unreported data from Time 1 and Time 2, observations from an additional 73 participants (Study 1: n = 25; Study 2: n = 48) who had been excluded from Cárdenas et al. (2021) for not providing Time 3 data, and novel analyses documenting associations across time points. As preregistered, we adopted a more conservative alpha level of .01 for null-hypothesis significance testing to account for the anticipated large size of the dataset.

Among participants who provided demographic data (n = 151 of 207), ages ranged from 18 to 62 years (M = 24.8, SD = 9.16); 117 identified as female, 29 as male, 2 as transgender, 1 as other, 2 preferred not to say. Participants were ethnically diverse with 55 identifying as Hispanic or Latina/o, 52 as White, 30 as Black or African American, 22 as Asian, 5 as Other.

When asked their employment status, 48 were employed part-time, 23 were employed full-time, 17 were unemployed and looking for work, 7 were self-employed, 5 were graduate students, 1 was in the military, 1 was unable to work, and 49 were undergraduate students. Ninety-one had completed some college or a two-year degree, 29 had completed college, 18 had a high school diploma, 12 had a professional degree, and 1 had a doctorate. See also "Supplemental Material: Demographic Information for the Subset of Participants Who Completed Time 2 (n = 144)." Flow of Expected Routines to Sampled Behavior and Retrospective Reports Panel A. Time 1 Routine Expectations and Time 2 Sampled Occasions

Procedure

Time 1. Expected Routines for Time Periods

Expected Routine Content. Using an online survey, 207 participants separately reported the person (who?), action (what?), and setting (where?) they expected to be typical of their weekly routines for 16 one-hour periods per day, from 7 AM to 11 PM, across all 7 days of the week (when? ; 112 time periods total). This resulted in 18,736 time-period reports.

Participants were encouraged to consult their planners to increase the accuracy of their reported routines. Instructions indicated that participants should report what they would 'normally be doing as part of [their] weekly routine,' including multiple activities within a given one-hour period and any known recurring alternatives (e.g., 'On Wednesdays from 5 to 6 PM, I am usually at work and then the gym, except on the last Wednesday of the month, when I skip the gym and go to happy hour instead'). They were also instructed to indicate when they did not expect a routine for a particular one-hour period by writing 'varies.' Notably, Time 1 measured generalized expectations for recurring time periods rather than predictions for particular future dates. For exact instructions, see Supplemental Material S5.

Expected Typicality. For each time period, participants also rated the expected typicality of the described routine-i.e., how "likely it was to happen every week at the same time, place, and with the same people"-from 1 (Very Atypical) to 7 (Very Typical).

Time 2. Concurrent Reports of Sampled Occasions

Next, 144 participants completed an experience-sampling phase lasting 10 to 14 days.

Data collection occurred at different calendar times across 10 recruitment waves, with 3 to 28 participants per wave (see Supplemental Material S6). On average, experience sampling began 3.63 days after Time 1 (SD = 2.73, mode = 2, range = 0-11). During this phase, participants received 3-4 text messages per day at the beginning of an hour between 8 AM and 11 PM asking about their current behavior. The sampling window comprised the interval during which most offenses occurred in one archival sample of Canadian and U.S. cases involving alibi evidence (see Burke & Marion, 2012). For each message, participants were prompted to respond with 1) who they were with, 2) what they were doing, and 3) where they were, along with filler items about their current emotional state. To prevent rehearsal of their responses, participants were instructed to avoid discussing their messages and to delete them. If they could not respond within 45 minutes of receiving the message for whatever reason, they were asked to respond "defer." On average, each participant provided 28.5 concurrent reports (SD = 8.27, range = 7-51). After exclusions (discussed below), we retained 3,510 sampled occasions which averaged 24.38 eligible reports per participant.

Time 3. Retrospective Reports of Sampled Occasions

Selection of Sampled Occasions. Finally, just over a week later (M = 7.94 days, SD = 3.55: range: 1.77-35), 134 participants completed a personalized free-recall memory test asking them to recall their behavior during four occasions sampled at Time 2. For each participant, the source-study researchers selected two occasions on which sampled behavior had been mostly or completely consistent with the expected routine reported at Time 1 and two on which it had been mostly or completely inconsistent, prioritizing completely consistent and completely inconsistent occasions (see Expectation-Behavior Consistency under Measures).

Retrospective Recall Task. Participants were asked to imagine themselves as suspects in a criminal investigation and that the accuracy of their memory reports would serve as alibis supporting their innocence. Study 1 participants reported alibis remotely via a Qualtrics survey, whereas Study 2 participants reported alibis in the laboratory during an interview with a trained RA. To assist retrieval, participants first recalled a four-hour window (8:30 AM to 12:30 PM) containing the sampled one-hour window (e.g., 10 AM to 11 AM), before reporting their alibi for the target one-hour window. Instructions emphasized that participants should not rely on any external memory aids and that they should avoid guessing. For two of four sampled occasions, participants were cued only by the target one-hour window; for the other two sampled occasions, recall was elicited via a mental reinstatement of context procedure. This elicitation technique manipulation had no significant effect on recall accuracy (see Measures for how this was coded) in Cárdenas et al. (2021) and was not of interest in the current work. Nonetheless, consistent with our preregistration we account for it statistically in our confirmatory model (described below). In total, participants provided 507 retrospective reports: 111 participants provided four reports, 17 provided three, and six provided two; none provided only one.

Additionally, participants also reported on the quality of their memories and, in Study 1 only, indicated the frequency with which they used a daily planner to manage their schedules, and how often they had rehearsed their memories for the sampled occasions by looking at the text messages they had sent the researchers, as well as additional exploratory measures. For planner-use and event-rehearsal results, see Supplemental Materials S12-S15.

Time 4. Second Retrospective Reports of Sampled Occasions

Only Study 2 participants participated in Time 4 tasks. After Time 3, they were instructed to search for evidence to corroborate their alibis. Just over a week later (M = 8.42 days, SD = 1.48: range 7-13), they then provided a second retrospective report of their Time 2 activities for the same four sampled occasions via an online survey. Participants provided a total of 218 additional retrospective reports: 49 participants provided four reports, four provided three, and five provided two; none provided only one. Finally, participants answered additional questions completed by Study 1 participants at Time 3 (e.g., on their use of planners), as well as a novel question "Compared to your usual routine, how common was the above event?" (1 = very uncommon to7 = very common).

Cross-Time Consistency Measures

Expectation-Behavior Consistency. To assess expectation-behavior consistency, Cárdenas and colleagues (2021) compared each expected routine reported at Time 1 with behavior reported on the corresponding sampled occasion at Time 2. Pairs of trained research assistants coded whether domain-level content-i.e., details about person, action, and settingmatched across the two reports (0 = no,1 = yes); one of the original authors resolved disagreements. When participants reported multiple expected people, actions, or settings within a time period, a Time 2 sampled detail was coded as consistent if it matched any corresponding Time 1 detail reported for that domain and period. The authors summed the three domain-level codes to produce an expectation-behavior consistency score ranging from 0 to 3 for each sampled occasion. Higher scores indicated that sampled behavior matched the expected routine across more domains.

A mismatch therefore indicates that the expected routine did not describe behavior on the sampled occasion; it cannot establish whether participants could have anticipated a onetime disruption or whether the same time period would have matched on another week.

Interrater reliability across coder pairs ranged from αs = .78 to .90. For coding instructions, see http://osf.io/abf4t/ (Holliday, 2003; Strange et al., 2014). For examples, see Supplemental Material S16.

Recall Accuracy. To assess recall accuracy, Cárdenas and colleagues (2021) compared participants' retrospective reports at Time 3 and Time 4 with their Time 2 concurrent reports of behavior using the same person, action, and setting coding scheme. The authors summed the three domain-level codes to produce separate occasion-level accuracy scores for T2-T3 consistency and T2-T4 consistency, each ranging from 0 to 3. Higher scores indicated greater occasion-level consistency between what participants had actually been doing and what they retrospectively reported doing. Our preregistered analyses focus on T2-T3 recall accuracy because Time 4 reports followed an earlier retrieval attempt and an opportunity to seek corroborating evidence, complicating the interpretation of T2-T4 accuracy.

Schema Reliance.

Only Study 2 included domain-level schema-reliance codes. We operationalized schema reliance as a Time 3 or Time 4 report that matched the corresponding Time 1 expected routine.

Data Processing

Eligibility of Sampled Occasions. Concurrent reports at Time 2 were excluded if during Time 1 prospective reporting, the participant had indicated no routine or, less commonly, a partial routine, as no measure of expectation-behavior consistency could be calculated (k = 348 observations). We excluded another 1,694 reports because participants responded outside the specified 45-minute interval, indicated that they could not provide the requested information, or encountered technical or procedural problems that prevented them from receiving prompts. See Supplemental Material S2 for details on exclusion reasons. Supplemental Materials S7-S9 describe additional characteristics and the distributions of attempted sampling prompts and retained sampled occasions across time periods. Supplemental Materials S10-S11 show that excluded and retained Time 2 observations had similar Time 1 expected-typicality ratings and temporal characteristics. Source studies were completed by Spring 2018, before the widespread availability of large language models for survey completion had become a concern. Therefore, they did not include AI-specific procedures to prevent participants from submitting LLMgenerated responses.

Eligibility of Retrospective Reports.

Due to technical errors during data collection in the source studies (e.g., an interviewer accidentally asking about a one-hour window that had not been sampled), recall accuracy could not be calculated for 29 of 536 retrospective reports.

Additionally, technical errors prevented an expectation-behavior consistency score from being calculated for an additional 21 retrospective reports (e.g., at Time 3, the interviewer accidentally asked about a sampled occasion corresponding to a Time 1 period with no specific expected routine). We retained these reports because expected typicality and recall accuracy were available, and an expectation-behavior consistency score was not required for all preregistered analyses. See Supplemental Material S2.

Results

We report expected routines at the time-period and domain levels, and expectationbehavior consistency at the sampled-occasion and domain levels. Time-period-and sampledoccasion-level results aggregate across the person, action, and setting domains; domain-level results show each domain separately.

How Often Do People Expect Routines During Specific Time Periods?

Time-Period Level. Across 18,736 time-period reports covering 7 AM to 11 PM, 207 participants reported a complete expected routine across the person, action, and setting domains for 92.83% of periods (k = 17,392). They reported an expected routine for two of the three domains for 2.51% (k = 470), for only one domain for 1.13% (k = 212), and no routine for any domain for 3.53% (k = 662) of time periods.

Domain Level.

At the domain level, participants reported routine expectations for the person, action, and setting domains in 96.29%, 93.50%, and 94.83% of time periods, respectively.

Expected Typicality.

Expected typicality ratings were also high, M = 6.26 (Mdn = 7, SD = 1.16). Most time periods (77.92%; k = 14,600) were rated as highly typical (6 or 7), whereas only 1.56% (k = 292) were rated as highly atypical (1 or 2). Thus, people believed they had highly typical routines for nearly all queried time periods which excluded regular sleeping hours (11 PM to 7 AM).

Exploratory descriptive analyses show that although expected typicality ratings were generally high, this tendency did not characterize all participants to the same degree: nearly one third (29.95%; n = 62) had a mean rating below 6 (Figure 2). High mean typicality ratings were broadly similar across participant characteristics (age, gender, ethnicity, education, and employment status) and time-period characteristics (time of day and day of week; Supplemental Material S19). Results reported here are similar among participants who completed the Time 1 reporting task (155) and those who did not (52; see Supplemental Materials S17-S18).

When People Expect A Time Period To Be Highly Routine, How Often Does Behavior on a Sampled Occasion Match That Expectation?

Sampled-Occasion Level. Among the 2,665 of 3,510 (75.93%) sampled occasions corresponding to time periods previously rated as highly typical (6 or 7) at Time 1, sampled behavior matched an average of 1.36 of the three domains (SD = 1.01, Mdn = 1). Of these sampled occasions, 24.02% (k = 640) did not match the expected routine in any domain, 31.59% (k = 842) matched one domain, 29.19% (k = 778) matched two domains, and 15.20% (k = 405) matched all three domains. Thus, 44.39% of sampled occasions matched expectations across at least two of the three domains. Figure 3, Panel A compares the number of expected routine domains with the number matched by sampled behavior.

Domain Level.

Similarly, when examining each domain separately, of 2,665 sampled occasions with high expected-typicality ratings, 51.18% (1,364) matched the expected person, 55.35% (1,475) matched the expected setting, and 29.04% (774) matched the expected action.

Descriptively, participants were less consistent about what they would be doing than who or where they would be with. For a comparison of expected routines and the number that matched sampled behaviors within each domain, see Figure 3, Panel B.

Thus, even when participants rated their routines as highly typical, sampled behavior was often consistent with expectations in only some domains or none. The degree to which expected routines matched sampled behavior also varied across and within participants ( Figure 4). Exploratory analyses show that sampled behavior matched fewer expected domains among periods expected to be low to moderately typical (see Supplemental Material S20). Low expectation-behavior consistency was also common across all time-period characteristics, albeit lower for action information, Sundays, evenings, and afternoons (see Figures S21-S22).

Next, we assessed whether higher expected typicality ratings predicted greater expectation-behavior consistency. We fit a linear mixed-effects model predicting expectation-behavior consistency from expected typicality reported at Time 1. Per our preregistration, we included random intercepts for participants, recruitment wave (1-10), and time periods (95 dayand-hour combinations) to account for nesting. See Table 1. Robustness checks that addressed residual normality model violations produced the same substantive conclusions and are reported in Supplemental Materials S23-S27.

Characteristics of Selected Occasions and Reports.

Descriptively, expected typicality was similarly high for the sampled occasions later queried at Time 3 (M = 6.25, Mdn = 7, SD = 1.12). For example, 78.10% of selected Time 3 occasions corresponded to periods rated 6 or 7, compared with 77.72% of all Time 2 sampled occasions with available typicality ratings. Among the 486 sampled occasions with available expectation-behavior consistency data, 41.77% matched expectations in no domains and 40.33% matched across all three, compared with 25.04% and 14.02%, respectively, among all Time 2 sampled occasions (for further information, see Supplemental Material S28). This endpoint-heavy selection offered a clearer contrast between occasions when expectations accurately versus inaccurately described behavior, but meant that the analysis characterized results within the selected occasions rather than the naturally occurring distribution at Time 2. Moreover, recall accuracy varied substantially across the 507 retrospective reports: 21.9% were completely inaccurate, 18.3% were accurate at the level of a single domain, 27.6% were accurate at two domain levels, and 32.1% were fully accurate across all three domains (M = 1.70 out of 3, Mdn = 2, SD = 1.14). Because the selected set overrepresented occasions that fully matched expectations, which participants recalled more accurately, these percentages likely overrepresent accurate retrospective reports.

For the distribution of recall accuracy across expected typicality ratings, see Figure 5.

Main Analysis.

Next, we fit a mixed-effects model predicting recall accuracy from expected typicality, with random intercepts for participants and elicitation technique (time cue vs. mental reinstatement of context) as a covariate; technique was not significant. Within this end-point heavy set of sampled occasions, expected typicality did not reliably predict recall accuracy, p = .128. See Table 2.

Robustness Checks. We also conducted exploratory robustness checks of this result (see Supplemental Material S29). First, our preregistered research question implied that we would investigate whether expectation-behavior consistency might moderate this association, although the analysis code included in the same preregistration did not specify that interaction.

We therefore tested it exploratorily. We also examined whether the result changed after controlling for planner use, event rehearsal, and the delay between sampling and recall (original covariates used in Cárdenas et al., 2021); modeling recall accuracy as an ordinal outcome to account for the skewed distribution; or allowing the association to differ across person, action, and setting domains. All robustness checks yielded substantively similar null results, although equivalence testing was inconclusive (see Supplemental Materials S1 and S29). horizontal lines indicate medians. Individual jittered points are overlaid to show the full spread of observations.

Exploratory Analysis: Do Stronger Routine Expectations Reappear in Later Reports?

People often rely on their routine knowledge of what usually happens when recalling an occasion that differed from their expectations (e.g., Leins & Charman, 2016). Here, we asked how often later reports repeated an expected detail that had not matched sampled behavior and whether people were more likely to do so when they had rated the routine as more typical. To answer these questions, we restricted the analysis to person, action, or setting domains in which the Time 1 expected detail differed from the Time 2 sampled detail. This allowed occasions with one or more mismatching details to contribute only the relevant domains. We coded schema reliance when the Time 3 retrospective report matched the Time 1 expectation within one of those domains. Because the original authors did not code Time 1-Time 3 consistency in Study 1, this analysis includes only Study 2 data. The analytic sample contained 328 domain-level observations from 126 sampled occasions reported by 59 participants.

Descriptively, participants showed schema reliance for 33.84% (111 of 328) of these expectation-inconsistent domain-level observations.

We fit a mixed-effects logistic regression predicting schema reliance (T1-T3 consistency) from expected typicality (1 to 7) while adjusting for domain type (person, action, setting). A random intercept for sampled occasion accounted for multiple domain-level observations from the same occasion unique to each participant (e.g., Tuesday, 1 to 2 PM for JJID 101; 126 total).

Higher expected typicality predicted greater schema reliance, b = 1.13, SE = 0.34, z = 3.34, p < .001, OR = 3.08, 95% CI [1.59, 5.96]. Each one-point increase in expected typicality was associated with approximately three times greater odds of schema reliance. Adding interactions between expected typicality and domain type did not improve model fit, χ²(2) = 0.64, p = .724.

Thus, the association did not reliably differ across person, action, and setting domains (see Supplemental Material S30).

General Discussion

When previously engaged in expectation-consistent behaviors, expectations about one's routines can help people reconstruct the past (e.g., Leins & Charman, 2016). However, we show that behavior matches time-specific routine expectations much less often than people assume. Regardless of participant-and time-period-level characteristics, participants reported expected routines for nearly all queried periods across all domains and rated most as highly typical, yet sampled occasions-particularly people's actions-infrequently unfolded as expected. Subjective ratings of expected typicality weakly predicted expectation-behavior consistency. When expectations differed from the sampled behavior, higher expected typicality predicted greater inaccurate reliance on routine knowledge in retrospective reports.

Together, these results suggest that routine expectations may make what would usually have happened seem plausible even when they do not describe the sampled occasion. These results are consistent with metacognitive accounts of autobiographical belief and empirical research suggesting that, when direct recollection is difficult, people sometimes report their expected behaviors for that period rather than what they were actually doing (Charman et al., 2019).

This phenomenon may be especially consequential in criminal investigations, where innocent suspects must account for their behavior during a specified period on a particular past date (Crozier et al., 2017). Relying on what one usually does may seem reasonable as it can produce a broadly plausible and accurate account when behavior during that period had been expectation-consistent. The current work suggests, however, that such reliance can mislead because innocent suspects may overestimate how reliably their usual behaviors occur at expected times. Reports based on confident reliance on expectations of routine may therefore systematically bias alibis toward providing expectation-consistent, but inaccurate details.

Limitations

Several limitations warrant consideration. First, our analyses concern what participants ultimately reported and cannot rule out whether routine knowledge sometimes helped them remember what actually happened when an occasion deviated from the routine. Second, because the sample included many students, the findings may not generalize to adults with different work, family, and recreational routines, although the student sample came from an urban commuter campus and most participants worked at least part time. Third, we did not sample the same time period for each participant across multiple weeks. Our findings therefore show how often routine expectations matched sampled occasions, not how often participants followed each routine over time.

Fourth, some sampled occasions lacked usable concurrent reports at Time 2, raising concern that report availability may have depended on what participants were doing. Somewhat lessening this concern, excluded and retained periods had similar Time 1 expected-typicality ratings and occurred on similar weekdays and at similar times of day (see Supplemental Materials S10-S11). However, if activities that deviated from expected routines were less likely to yield usable reports, retained observations may overstate how often sampled behavior was consistent with expectations. Yet routine activities such as sleeping, working, or attending class could also impede responding, leaving the direction and magnitude of any selection bias unclear.

Fifth, real-time reporting may have made sampled occasions more memorable.

However, prior work suggests minimal effects of such reporting on memory (Thompson, 1982), participants recalled only four of approximately 28 sampled occasions, and controlling for selfreported event rehearsal did not substantively change the present results. Finally, reporting routines across an entire week of time periods was demanding and may have encouraged loweffort responses. This concern is reduced, though not eliminated, by supplemental analyses. Time 1 expected-typicality ratings showed modest correspondence with Time 4 commonness ratings, and participants often reproduced the same expected details across reports (see Supplemental Materials S31-32). Even participants who did not complete the full Time 1 routinereporting task described their lives as highly routine. Therefore, non-completion was unlikely to indicate disengagement resulting from having either unusually many routines to report or unusually few.

Future Directions

Future work should better distinguish between misattribution errors in prospective reports of expected routines and retrospective reports (Rubínová & Kontogianni, 2023). In prospective reports, participants may have described real routines that occur at a different time than the one queried or only at a broader temporal scale (e.g., "in the morning" rather than 9-10 AM). In retrospective reports, they may have reported real events-routine or not-that occurred outside the target interval. These possibilities are consistent with time-slice errors, such as choosing the correct day but wrong week or the correct hour but wrong day (Laliberte et al., 2021), and telescoping errors in which events from outside a reporting interval are misdated as occurring within it (Neter & Waksberg, 1964; Rubin & Baddeley, 1989). Regardless of when the errors arose, routine-based inference may still be a poor guide to what happened during a particular occasion.

Future studies could repeatedly sample the same time periods to estimate how consistently individual routines recur. Experiments could also manipulate the strength of a timespecific routine while holding a routine-inconsistent event constant, testing whether stronger routines improve memory for deviations or instead increase schema-consistent recall errors.

Conclusion

The current work suggests that people may be more confident in their knowledge of their routines than is warranted by their behavior on sampled occasions. Higher expected typicality did not improve retrospective recall accuracy; when sampled behavior deviated from expectations, higher expected typicality instead predicted greater schema reliance. Knowledge of one's routines may therefore provide a tempting basis for reconstructing the past. Yet given how often behavior on sampled occasions diverged from expected routines, routine knowledge should be critically evaluated; otherwise, it may prematurely end the search for episode-specific details and lead people to report an inference as though it were a memory.

The research question, as written, is inconsistent with the analysis we preregistered we would perform. The analysis does not account for the moderating effect of routine consistency (i.e., "typicality vs. atypicality of the events").

We retained the specified model as our primary model (reported in manuscript) and conducted an exploratory analysis examining whether routine consistency moderated this association. Results were consistent with those reported in the paper. Expected typicality did not reliably predict accuracy in the preregistered model and the exploratory analysis indicated that this association did not significantly differ by routine consistency, b = 0.22, SE = 0.09, t(461.26) = 2.38, p = .018. (We preregistered a more conservative alpha of .01). Expected typicality did not reliably predict accuracy for relatively routine-inconsistent events, b = -0.08, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.20, 0.05], p = .241, or for relatively expectation-consistent events, b = 0.14, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [0.004, 0.28], p = .043.

We report results of both in provided materials.

4 Type Sampl e

We indicated expecting 152 participants for Time 1. ""The manuscript describes 152 participants (80 in Study 1 and 72 in Study 2) as having completed Phase 1 (T1 -Expected Routines)."

However, when we reviewed all available Time 1 data, we found that 207, not 152, participants had consented and provided any Time 1 responses (i.e., completed one or more of the 112 time periods). Cárdenas et al. reported the number of participants who "completed Phase 1" (p. 5). As such, we failed to account for participants who provided some, but not all, Time 1 responses in our estimate. However, In the supplemental materials, we report results of the smaller sample that completed Time 1 measures (112 time periods) and the complete sample. These are substantively consistent.

"Results for Subset of Participants Who Completed Time 1 (n = 155)" and "Potential Effects of Attrition at Time 1".

Error After data acces s we retained data from these additional 55 participants because doing so was consistent with our preregistration: "We will use data available at each phase, such that responses to expectations about routine events (T1) will correspond to a larger sample size than responses to memory test (T3)."

Of these 207 participants, 155 reported on all 112 time periods at Time 1. We recognize that 155 still differs from the 152 reported by Cárdenas et al. We suspect that, by "completed," Cárdenas et al. meant that a participant had completed all 112 time periods and provided contact information, primarily a phone number, which was necessary for the Phase 2 experience sampling.

Of these 155 participants, only 151 reached the end of the Time 1 survey, where the demographic questions were located. We cannot be completely certain why Cárdenas et al. reported that 152 rather than 151 participants completed Time 1.

The only variables omitted from the available Time 1 data concern participants' contact information, which was requested on the same page as the demographic questions. It is possible that 152 participants provided contact information and that this criterion determined who Cárdenas et al. counted as having completed Time 1.

In summary: • 155 participants reported on all 112 time periods.

• 151 participants provided demographic information.

• The source study reported that 152 participants completed Time 1; one additional participant may have provided contact information but not demographic information.

S3. Demographic Information for Subset of Participants Who Completed Time 2 (n = 144)

Demographics in the manuscript are reported for a subset of the sample of participants who completed Time 1 (i.e., prospective reporting of expected behaviors) and provided demographic data at the end of that session (n = 151). Descriptively, demographic information did not differ among the subset of participants who later contributed Time 2 data (n = 144), ages ranged from 18 to 59 years (M = 24.18, SD = 8.27). Of these participants, 110 identified as female, 27 as male, 2 as transgender, 1 as other, and 2 preferred not to say. Participants were ethnically diverse: Among the 142 who provided ethnicity data, 53 identified as Hispanic or Latino/a, 49 as White, 28 as Black or African American, 19 as Asian, and 5 as Other. When asked their employment status, 47 identified as undergraduate students, 46 were employed part-time, 20 were employed full-time, 16 were unemployed and looking for work, 7 were selfemployed, 4 were graduate students, 1 was in the military, and 1 was unable to work. With respect to education, 71 reported some college, 29 had completed a 4-year degree, 17 were high school graduates, 14 had completed a 2-year degree, and 11 had a professional degree. Emotions. Emotion ratings collected as filler items were collected for both source studies. However, these were only available for the present analyses from Study 2 data.

Participants reported feeling moderately happy during sampled events (M = 4.53 of 7, SD = 1.53, Mdn = 5, n = 1,689). Sadness ratings were lower on average (M = 2.48, SD = 1.71, Mdn = 2, n = 1,606). The distribution of sadness ratings was positively skewed, indicating that most events were rated as low in sadness. the Time 1 heatmap, which summarizes participants' prospective routine expectations across all queried weekly time periods, this figure summarizes only Time 2 events that were actually sampled and deemed eligible for inclusion. These events were distributed across 95 unique time periods out of 112 possible periods from 8:00 AM to 11:00 PM. Most eligible Concurrent Reports at Time 2 occurred in the evening (43.65%) or afternoon (37.12%), with fewer reports in the morning (19.23%). Eligible reports were sampled across all days of the week, with the largest proportions occurring on Monday (18.52%) and Tuesday (16.30%) and the smallest proportions occurring on Friday (11.17%) and Saturday (11.28%). See Supplemental Material S2 for reasons for missing data.

S10. Comparisons Between Excluded And Retained Concurrent Reports at Time 2

Because a substantial number of Time 2 periods were excluded from analyses, it is important to consider whether those exclusions introduced systematic bias into the experiencesampling data reported in the manuscript. Several comparisons suggest that the excluded periods were broadly similar to the retained periods. First, typicality ratings for excluded timeperiods (k = 2,042, M = 6.14, SD = 1.81) were largely similar to ratings for retained time-periods (k = 3,510, M = 6.2, SD = 1.16). Second, excluded time-periods occurred at similar times of days as retained time-periods (see Supplemental Material S11, Panel A). Third, the distribution for days of the week when excluded time-periods occurred was mostly comparable to that of retained time-periods, with the exception of Sunday which accounted for 5% more of excluded than retained time-periods (20% vs. 15%) and Thursday, which accounted for approximate 5% fewer of excluded than retained time-periods (9.45% vs. 14.2%). See Supplemental Material S11, Panel B. Additionally, planner use was not significantly associated with the mean amount of expected routine information (0 to 3) participants reported at Time 1, r(120) = -.13 [-.31, .04], p = .139, or with their mean typicality ratings, r(120) = .06 [-.11, .24], p = .478 S13.

S17. Results for Subset of Participants Who Completed Time 1 (n = 155)

In main analyses we report data from any participants who reported prospective routines (or lack thereof) for at least one time period (N = 207). Of those, 155 (75%) reported on potential routines for 100% of 112 time periods queried. The number of time periods from this subset of participants was 17,360.

Results concerning expected routines and expected typicality for this smaller subset were consistent with those reported in the manuscript for the full sample. Across 17,360 time periods, participants reported a full expected routine across the person, action, and setting domains for 92.40% (k = 16,041) and no expected routine for 3.73% (k = 647). Expectedtypicality ratings were high on average (M = 6.26, Mdn = 7, SD = 1.14): participants rated 77.94% (k = 13,531) of time periods as highly typical (6 or 7) and 1.47% (k = 255) as highly atypical (1 or 2).

S18. Potential Effects of Attrition at Time 1

At Time 1, 155 of 207 participants reported whether they expected routine events for all 112 queried time periods. The remaining 52 participants provided partial prospective reports, most often discontinuing after completing the Monday time periods (36 of 52 participants). We compared completers and non-completers on the measures most important to the current work.

Both groups described their lives as highly routine. Non-completers reported information for an average of 2.96 of the 3 routine domain levels (i.e., person, action, setting) per time period (SD = 0.32, Mdn = 3), compared with 2.84 among completers (SD = 0.62, Mdn = 3), a small difference, d = 0.20 [0.15, 0.26]. Expected typicality ratings were also highly similar across groups. Non-completers' average expected typicality rating was 6.19 out of 7 (SD = 1.30, Mdn = 7), compared with 6.26 among completers (SD = 1.14, Mdn = 7), d = 0.06 [0.00, 0.11]. These comparisons likely somewhat overestimate non-completers' expected routines because task progress was confounded with day of week: participants completed the planner in Monday-to-Sunday order, and Monday-Thursday periods tended to receive slightly higher typicality ratings than Friday-Sunday periods (see S19).

We also examined whether task progress (0 to 100%) was associated with the average number of routine domain information reported per event (0 to 3) or with expected typicality (1 to 7). Task progress refers to a Qualtrics-generated measure of the extent of progress a survey taker made before discontinuing a survey. Task progress showed a very small negative association with routine domain information, b = -0.002, SE < 0.001, t(225.50) = -2.20, p = .029, such that each 10-percentage-point increase in survey completion corresponded to a negligible 0.02 fewer routine domains on the 0 to 3 scale. Of note, this result did not meet our preregistered alpha level of .01. Task progress was not associated with expected typicality, b = 0.001, SE = 0.002, t(216.10) = 0.70, p = .483. In sum, the tendency to describe life as highly routine was not limited to participants who completed all Time 1 reports.

S20. Expectation-Behavior Consistency for Low-to-Moderately Typical Periods

When people expect a time period to be low to moderately routine, how often does their actual behavior align with their expectation? Among the 764 of 3,510 experience-sampled events that participants had rated as low to moderately typical (1 to 5) at Time 1, even fewer events occurred as expected than among events rated as highly typical. Only 9.82% (k = 75) events were completely consistent with prospectively expected routines across all three coded domains, and 25% (k = 191) were consistent across two of three domains. In contrast, 37.04 (k = 283) matched across only one domain, and 28.14% (k = 215) did not match any domain.

S26. Ordinal Robustness Check of Effect of Typicality on Expectation-Behavior Consistency

Because the model predicting expectation-behavior consistency showed that residual normality was violated, we fit our data to a cumulative link mixed model accounting for the ordinal structure of the data. This ordinal robustness check produced the same conclusion as the primary model. Expected typicality again significantly predicted expectation-behavior consistency, b = 0.18, SE = 0.03, z = 5.21, p < .001.

S29.4 Equivalence Testing of Null Effect on Recall Accuracy at Time 3

To assess the robustness of the null finding for the effect of expected typicality on recall accuracy, we conducted a test of equivalence. Consistent with Cárdenas et al. (2021), we defined the smallest effect size of interest as half a detail on the 0 to 3 accuracy scale. This is equivalent to a slope bound of ±0.083, or a change of 0.5 units across the full 7-point expected typicality scale. The slope-based TOST was inconclusive, b = 0.08, SE = 0.05, p > .05. We could reject effects more negative than -0.083, t(505) = 3.63, p < .001, but could not reject effects larger than +0.083, t(505) = -0.07, p = .473. Thus, this analysis did not provide evidence that the effect of expected typicality on recall accuracy was statistically equivalent to zero.

S29.5 Does the Effect of Typicality on Recall Accuracy Depend on Domain Type?

Given the null finding for the effect of typicality on recall accuracy at the global level (when aggregating person, setting, action domain levels), we examined whether typicality influenced recall accuracy at the level of detail. We fit a mixed-effects model predicting accuracy at the level of detail with a random intercept for participants. This yielded a sample of 1521 pieces of domain-level information (from 507 alibis). Once again, expected typicality did not predict accuracy of the retrospective report, b = 0.02, SE = 0.01, t(868.40) = 1.33, p = .183.

There was a main effect of domain type: tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons showed that person details were recalled more accurately than action details, p < .001, and setting details were recalled more accurately than action details, p < .001, whereas person and setting details did not differ, p = .607. Finally, the interaction of typicality and domain type did not improve model fit, χ²(2) = 0.01, p = .995. See Supplemental Material S22, Panel B.

S31. Consistency of Routine Expectations

Were participants' beliefs about the routine nature of their life consistent across time? To answer this question we examined objective and subjective sources of information, including the degree to which participants reproduced similar domain information (across person, setting, and action domains) across time and the consistency between their prospective and retrospective reports of expected typicality.

First, we found that participants often reiterated the same expected detail over time. To directly test whether their routine-based reports were similar across time, we isolated cases where participants' original routine was wrong and then asked whether they repeated that same wrong detail later. To examine this, we identified cases in which a detail (person, setting, action) participants expected at Time 1 did not match what actually occurred at Time 2 and was also reported inaccurately at Time 3. We then asked whether the inaccurate Time 3 detail nevertheless matched the original Time 1 expectation. 1 It did in 43.7% of cases (87 of 199), indicating that even when participants were wrong, they still reproduced an expectationconsistent detail nearly half the time. This tendency was similar for person-level information (49.1%) and setting-level information (48.5%), and somewhat lower for action-level information (35.1%). At the alibi level, 52% of inaccurate reports about sampled occasions that matched expectations in no domains nevertheless included at least one detail from the participant's expected routine. At Time 4, participants continued to make expectation-consistent errors in 37.3% of cases (69 of 185), suggesting continued, though reduced, reliance on schemas.

Second, we examined the consistency of perceived routineness at a more subjective level at Time 1 and at Time 4. Two caveats apply to this analysis. First, the Time 1 and Time 4 1 Note that this analysis relies on a different subset of participants from the exploratory analysis reported in the manuscript on the relation of report inaccuracy to schema reliance.

Here we included both prospective reports that had been and that had not been consistent with concurrent reports (i.e., expectation-behavioral consistency scores of 0 and 1, at the domain-level, were included).

S4. Student-Community Comparisons

Among the source studies, Study 1 recruited required participants to be college students (n = 99), whereas Study 2 did not (n = 108). In Study 2, 16 participants indicated being community members recruited via Craigslist, whereas 44 were recruited via undergraduates recruited via flyers posted on college campuses. Data are missing for the other 48 participants who completed some portion of Study 2 Time 1. Reported typicality in the subset of events recalled during Time 3 did not differ across the student and community member samples.

Community members reported similarly high typicality (estimated marginal means = 6.12, SE = 0.19) as the student sample (estimated marginal means = 6.29, SE = 0.06), and sample type was not a significant predictor of typicality according to a mixed effects model accounting for byparticipant variation, b = 0.17, SE = 0.20, t(157.45) = 0.87, p = .385. Additionally, community members showed similar expectation-behavior consistency scores (T1-T2 consistency) (estimated marginal means = 1.42, SE = 0.08) as students (estimated marginal means = 1.30, SE = 0.03). Sample type was not a significant predictor of consistency, b = -0.12, SE = 0.08, t(138.27) = -1.41, p = .161.

S23. Domain Differences in the Expected-Typicality and Expectation-Behavior Consistency Association

Does the effect of typicality on expectation-behavior consistency differ based on domain type? Descriptively, people were better able to predict where they would be (k = 3,510, M = .54, SD = .50) and who they would be with (k = 3, 510, M = .51, SD = .50) than what they would be doing (k = 3,510, M = .27, SD = .44). We conducted exploratory analyses to assess whether the relation between expected typicality and expectation-behavior consistency depended on the type of detail reported. In a mixed-effects model with random intercepts for participants and fixed effects for both typicality and domain type, higher typicality predicted greater overall Adding the Typicality by Type of Domain Type interaction did not improve model fit, χ²(2) = 2.26, p = .322, indicating that the effect of typicality on expectation-behavior consistency did not significantly differ across person-, action-, and setting-level information. See Supplemental Material S22, Panel A.

S25. Model Assumption Checks

We inspected model diagnostics for the two primary linear mixed-effects models. For the model predicting expectation-behavior consistency, the model was not singular, and there was no evidence of heteroscedasticity, p = .767. However, residual normality was violated, p < .001.

For the model predicting retrospective report accuracy at Time 3, there was no evidence of multicollinearity, VIFs = 1.00, the model was not singular, and there was no evidence of heteroscedasticity, p = .439. Residual normality was again violated, p < .001. These deviations may be due to the bounded nature of consistency scores (ranging from 0 to 3). To examine the robustness of the preregistered analyses we reran the primary models as cumulative link mixed models, treating outcome variables as ordered categories. Results were consistent with the conclusions reported based on the primary models: Expected typicality predicted later expectation-behavior consistency, but did not reliably predict retrospective report accuracy. For regression output, see "Ordinal Robustness Checks" sections below.

S29.1 Ordinal Robustness Check of Effect of Typicality on Recall Accuracy

Because the model predicting recall accuracy showed that residual normality was violated, we ran fit our data to a cumulative link mixed model accounting for the ordinal structure of the data. This ordinal robustness check produced the same conclusion as the primary model.

Expected typicality did not significantly predict retrospective report accuracy, b = 0.12, SE = 0.08, z = 1.57, p = .116. The recall technique covariate was also not significant, b = 0.06, SE = 0.16, z = 0.38, p = .706.

S29.2 Effect of Typicality on Recall Accuracy at Time 3, Not Controlling for Covariates

In our preregistration, we specified a mixed-effects model predicting recall accuracy (0-3) for 507 alibis from expected typicality ratings, controlling for recall method and including random intercepts for study and participants. The study-level random intercept produced a singular fit and contributed less than .001 variance, so it was removed from the final model.

Here, we report the more parsimonious model without the covariate to show that the results were substantively unchanged. Consistent with the result reported in manuscript, expected typicality did not predict recall accuracy, b = 0.07, SE = 0.05, t(404.48) = 1.53, p = .126.

S29.3 Effect of Typicality on Recall Accuracy at Time 3, Controlling for Cárdenas et al. (2021) Covariates

As a robustness check, we also fit the model including the covariates used by Cárdenas et al. (2021), event rehearsal, planner use, and delay between when the sampled occasion occurred and the recall test. Results were virtually identical with no effect of typicality, b = 0.07, SE = 0.05, t(372.92) = 1.39, p = .164; recall method was also not significant, b = 0.02, SE = 0.10, t(352.74) = 0.19, p = .846; nor was planner use, b = 0.04, SE = 0.04, t(119.82) = 0.99, p = .323, delay interval between Time 2 and Time 3, b = -0.01, SE = 0.01, t(460.98) = -0.82, p = .415, or event rehearsal, b = -0.08, SE = 0.04, t(122.63) = -2.27, p = .025. Notably, although this

S29.6 Does Expectation-Behavior Consistency Moderate the Association Between Expected Typicality and Recall Accuracy?

We note in the limitations that the source studies deliberately selected Time 3 occasions that overrepresented complete matches and mismatches between expected routines and sampled behavior (i.e., expectation-behavior consistency scores of 0 and 3). This offered unambiguous within-participant examples in which routine knowledge was either an accurate or misleading basis for reconstruction. However, partially matching occasions, although more common during experience sampling, were underrepresented. Consequently, the present analyses offer limited evidence about whether expected typicality predicts recall accuracy for partially expectation-consistent occasions.

This limitation raises the possibility that the overall association between expected typicality (1 to 7) and recall accuracy (0 to 3) may not capture associations within relatively expectation-consistent and expectation-inconsistent events. To formally examine this possibility, we conducted an exploratory moderation analysis.

While considering this analysis, we noticed an inconsistency in our preregistration materials, which we now report as Item 3 in our preregistration deviations disclosure table . Our preregistered research question referred to a potential moderating effect of expectationbehavior consistency on the association between expected typicality and recall accuracy (i.e., "How well do ratings of expected typicality of behaviors predict accuracy of recall for typical vs.

atypical events?"), but the model code specified for this question tested only the overall association between expected typicality and recall accuracy (i.e., Recall Accuracy ~ Expected Typicality). That is, the code did not include the moderating effect of expectation-behavior consistency. For transparency, we conducted an exploratory moderation analysis in which we grouped relatively routine-inconsistent events (scores of 0 or 1) and expectation-consistent events (scores of 2 or 3), consistent with the criteria used to select the memory-test events in the source studies and the language of the preregistration.

The exploratory moderation analysis yielded substantively similar conclusions to the primary analysis. The interaction between expected typicality and expectation-behavior consistency did not meet our preregistered alpha criterion of .01, b = 0.22, SE = 0.09, t(461.26) = 2.38, p = .018. Expected typicality did not reliably predict accuracy for relatively expectationinconsistent events, b = -0.08, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.20, 0.05], p = .241, or relatively expectation-consistent events, b = 0.14, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [0.004, 0.28], p = .043.

ratings were conceptually similar but not identical. At Time 1, participants rated how typical each expected event was of their routine (1 = very atypical,7 = very typical), whereas at Time 4 they rated how common the reported event was compared with their usual routine (1 = very uncommon,7 = very common). Second, only Study 2 participants completed the Time 4 commonness rating.

For a more direct comparison, we first report on expected typicality at Time 1 among only the subset of time periods queried at Time 3 in Study 2 (k = 226 versus the entire corpus of 18,736 periods). Expected typicality at Time 1 was high (M = 6.27, Mdn = 7, SD = 1.02), with 77.43% (175 of 226) rated 6 or 7. Time 4 commonness ratings were lower (M = 5.35, Mdn = 6, SD = 1.74), with 55.31% (125 of 226) rated 6 or 7. However, this difference in typicality is not especially surprising because half of the Time 2 events were intentionally selected because they highly deviates from participants' routine expectations. The more notable question is why this proportion was not lower. One possibility is that participants relied on routine-based schemas when retrospectively reporting even schema-inconsistent events, consistent with prior work showing that people use routine knowledge to reconstruct the past (Cárdenas et al., 2021; Eastwood et al., 2021; Leins et al., 2016). Thus, the present findings suggest that people may overestimate the routineness of their behavior both prospectively and retrospectively.

We then formally tested whether participants' Time 4 commonness ratings were related to their original Time 1 typicality ratings. Accounting for by-participant variation, a mixed-effects model with random intercepts for participants indicated a small but significant positive association between Time 4 commonness and Time 1 typicality ratings, b = 0.10, SE = 0.04, t(223.35) = 2.62, p = .009. Still, the persistence of relatively high Time 4 commonness ratings suggests that participants revised their routine judgments only partially, even after reporting on events that were often selected because they contradicted their original expectations.

Domain type also significantly predicted expectation-behavior consistency. When averaging across degrees of expected typicality, action-level information was less likely to match participants' later experience-sampled reports than person-level information, b = -0.23, SE = 0.01, z = -20.56, p < .001, and setting-level information, b = -0.26, SE = 0.01, z = -23.17, p < .001.
